purpose: Evidence-based environmental disease and pest risk forecasting using literature-derived rules, published epidemiological models and weather data.

forecasting_scope.extended_projection: 30-day risk outlook, not deterministic weather forecast
forecasting_scope.impact_output: Literature-supported untreated loss and managed-loss / yield-preservation scenarios only where credible evidence exists.

temperature.notes: TNAU crop-protection guidance reports moderate temperatures around 25–28°C as favorable for Alternaria leaf spot.

relative_humidity.notes: High humidity favors Alternaria leaf spot development.

rainfall.notes: Intermittent rains and humid conditions favor disease development. No universal rainfall cutoff is frozen.

rules.description: Temperature around 25–28°C increases disease suitability.
High relative humidity increases disease suitability.
Intermittent rainfall or prolonged wet conditions strengthen disease pressure.
Current confirmed disease detection increases operational case risk.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: Field evidence supports weather–disease relationships, but a generalized deployment-grade yield-loss percentage has not yet been verified.

limitations: Risk represents environmental favorability rather than a guaranteed disease outbreak.
Rainfall effects depend on local crop canopy and duration of wetness.
Exact loss percentages are not currently supported.

temperature.notes: Published Indian bacterial-blight prediction work used weather variables together with historical disease incidence. No single universal temperature interval is frozen here.

relative_humidity.notes: Humidity is retained as a disease-pressure variable based on published Indian prediction studies.

rainfall.notes: Rainfall is treated as a contributing disease-pressure factor. A fixed universal rainfall threshold is not assigned.

published_model.output_interpretation: Disease-incidence prediction relationship reported across Indian locations.
published_model.location_relevance: Indian multi-location evidence; exact deployment equation/raw data are not currently available in machine-readable form.

rules.description: Weather favorability should be interpreted together with recent or historical disease presence.
Rainfall and humidity increase disease pressure when other conditions are favorable.
Current confirmed bacterial-blight detection increases case-specific risk.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: Current evidence supports disease forecasting relationships but does not yet provide a safely generalized yield-loss range for farmer-facing use.

limitations: The original raw model-development dataset is not currently available.
The published model should not be treated as a calibrated local probability for Yavatmal without validation.
Historical disease incidence is an important predictor and may be unavailable for first-time users.

temperature.notes: The uploaded historical Indian study of spotted bollworm reported high infestation around minimum temperatures of approximately 19–20°C and maximum temperatures around 30–32°C.

relative_humidity.notes: The spotted-bollworm study reported high morning relative humidity around 95–100% during periods associated with maximum infestation.

rainfall.notes: The historical study reported weekly rainfall around 170–210 mm during periods of maximum spotted-bollworm infestation. This is study-specific evidence and is not treated as a universal threshold.

sunshine.notes: The study reported approximately 5–7 hours of bright sunshine during periods associated with higher spotted-bollworm infestation.

variables: X1 = weekly mean minimum temperature for 43rd standard week
X2 = weekly maximum temperature for 50th standard week
X3 = morning relative humidity for 34th standard week
X4 = bright sunshine hours for 30th standard week
published_model.output_interpretation: Published relationship with percentage infestation of spotted bollworm.
published_model.location_relevance: Historical field study from Surat, Gujarat. Useful as supporting meteorological evidence, but not a direct species-general model for Yavatmal cotton.

rules.description: Temperature conditions resembling the published spotted-bollworm high-infestation range increase meteorological suitability.
Very high morning relative humidity increases suitability according to the spotted-bollworm study.
Rainfall and sunshine are treated as supporting factors using the historical meteorological evidence.
Species-specific forecasting must not be presented until the bollworm species is confirmed by an Extension Officer or expert.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: The current historical source reports percentage infestation, not a directly transferable crop-yield-loss percentage.

limitations: Model 1 detects generic cotton bollworm and does not identify the bollworm species.
The available meteorological paper specifically concerns spotted bollworm (Earias spp.).
Species-specific risk and management must not be shown as definitive until expert verification.
The regression uses standard-week-specific variables and should not be blindly applied as a daily universal equation.

rules.description: Healthy image detection triggers preventive monitoring rather than treatment.
Environmental pressure may still be evaluated separately for Alternaria, bacterial blight and bollworm.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: No crop-loss estimate is generated for a healthy detection.

limitations: A healthy image does not prove the entire cotton field is disease- or pest-free.
Preventive environmental monitoring should continue when conditions become favorable.

temperature.notes: Government grape disease guidance reports favorable development around 25–30°C.

relative_humidity.notes: High relative humidity around 80–90% is reported as favorable for bacterial leaf spot development.

rainfall.notes: Wet and humid periods increase environmental suitability. No fixed rainfall threshold is assigned because the source does not justify one.

rules.description: Temperature within 25–30°C increases environmental suitability.
Relative humidity >=80% increases environmental suitability.
Wet/rainy conditions strengthen risk when temperature and humidity are already favorable.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: Current evidence supports disease occurrence and environmental suitability but does not yet provide a reliable generalized yield-loss percentage for deployment.

limitations: Risk output represents environmental suitability, not laboratory-confirmed disease progression.
No fixed rainfall threshold is currently supported.
Biological-control evidence from ICAR-NRC Grapes-linked laboratory work is in-vitro only and is not converted into field treatment prescriptions.

temperature.notes: Temperature is used together with wetness/moisture conditions in published grape downy mildew infection models. No single universal temperature interval is frozen here.

relative_humidity.notes: High humidity supports infection risk, but humidity alone is insufficient for forecasting.

rainfall.notes: Rainfall and prolonged wet periods strongly increase risk. Published models emphasize wetness duration and temperature during wetness rather than a universal rainfall cutoff.

leaf_wetness.notes: Leaf wetness duration is a key predictor in published downy mildew infection models. If direct leaf-wetness data are unavailable, rainfall and sustained high humidity may be used only as proxies.

published_model.output_interpretation: Relative infection risk under favorable wetness and temperature conditions.
published_model.location_relevance: External grape disease model; requires local validation before quantitative deployment in Maharashtra.

rules.description: Longer leaf-wetness duration increases infection risk.
Temperature during wet periods modifies infection suitability.
Rainfall or sustained high humidity can act as proxy evidence for wetness when direct leaf-wetness data are unavailable.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: No deployment-grade generalized yield-loss range has yet been verified for this disease-crop-location combination.

limitations: Direct leaf-wetness duration may not be available from the weather API.
Rainfall and humidity used as wetness proxies introduce uncertainty.
External published infection models require local calibration for Maharashtra.

rules.description: Healthy detection triggers preventive monitoring rather than treatment.
The system may still calculate environmental disease pressure for major grape diseases using separate disease-risk modules.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: No crop-loss estimate is generated for a healthy detection.

limitations: Healthy image classification does not prove the entire vineyard is disease-free.
Preventive monitoring should continue when environmental conditions become favorable for disease.

temperature.notes: Temperature is a major driver of powdery mildew risk, but no universal interval is frozen here without a locally validated source-specific threshold.

relative_humidity.notes: Humidity affects powdery mildew development. Risk logic should use the disease-specific published guidance rather than a generic high-humidity threshold.

rainfall.notes: Rainfall is considered as a modifying factor, but is not treated the same way as downy mildew.

rules.description: Temperature suitability contributes to powdery mildew risk.
Humidity modifies disease suitability.
Recent disease detection increases operational case risk even when environmental conditions become less favorable.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: No verified generalized yield-loss percentage is currently frozen for product use.

limitations: Current grape longitudinal dataset was not accepted as the deployment basis because strong seasonality dominated supervised ML performance.
Risk output should therefore be interpreted as epidemiological environmental suitability rather than an ML disease probability.

rules.description: Healthy image detection triggers preventive monitoring rather than treatment.
Environmental pressure may still be monitored separately for Purple Blotch and Stemphylium Leaf Blight.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: No yield-loss estimate is generated for a healthy detection.

limitations: A healthy image does not prove that the entire onion field is disease-free.
Preventive monitoring should continue when weather becomes favorable for Purple Blotch or Stemphylium Leaf Blight.

temperature.notes: Indian agricultural literature reports approximately 20–25°C as favorable for purple blotch development.

relative_humidity.notes: Relative humidity above approximately 75% is reported as favorable for purple blotch development.

rainfall.notes: Rainfall and prolonged humid/wet conditions may favor disease development. No universal rainfall threshold is frozen.

published_model.model_type: Published field disease-weather relationship / regression evidence
published_model.output_interpretation: Environmental conditions associated with purple blotch disease progression.
published_model.location_relevance: Indian field evidence; suitable for rule design but still requires local calibration for exact quantitative risk probabilities.

rules.description: Temperature in the 20–25°C range increases environmental suitability.
Relative humidity >=75% increases environmental suitability.
Rainfall or prolonged wet/humid periods strengthen risk when temperature is favorable.
Current confirmed disease presence increases operational case risk.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: Current evidence supports disease progression and environmental favorability. A generalized untreated yield-loss percentage has not yet been frozen for deployment.

limitations: Risk represents environmental suitability and disease pressure, not a guaranteed outbreak probability.
Published field relationships may vary by cultivar, season and local agronomic practice.
No fixed rainfall cutoff is currently supported.

temperature.notes: A multi-season field study at Chitegaon Phata, Nashik reported approximately 16.25–22.5°C as favorable during Stemphylium leaf blight development.

relative_humidity.notes: The Nashik field study reported relative humidity around 85–90% during favorable disease development.

rainfall.notes: The published Nashik study focused primarily on temperature and relative humidity relationships. No independent rainfall threshold is frozen here.

published_model.model_type: Published stepwise regression / field epidemiological model
published_model.output_interpretation: Published regression relationship for disease intensity under specific seasonal conditions in the Nashik field study.
published_model.location_relevance: High relevance: developed from multi-season field observations at Chitegaon Phata, Nashik, Maharashtra.

rules.description: Mean/favorable temperature around 16.25–22.5°C increases environmental suitability.
Relative humidity around 85–90% increases disease suitability.
Published Nashik regression may be used as a supporting disease-pressure indicator when input variables and units match the original study.
Current confirmed infection raises case-specific operational risk.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: The current source reports percent disease intensity and AUDPC, but does not justify a generalized crop-yield-loss percentage for direct farmer display.

limitations: The published regression is study-specific and should not be interpreted directly as a calibrated probability.
Regression output must only be used when variable definitions and units match the source study.
Local cultivar, planting date and management practices may affect disease behavior.

temperature.notes: Published Indian early-blight forecasting work used temperature together with humidity, rainfall, sunshine and wind variables. No single universal temperature interval is frozen here.

relative_humidity.notes: FAST-type tomato early-blight models use periods of very high relative humidity, commonly above 90%, together with temperature and moisture conditions.

rainfall.notes: Rainfall contributes to prolonged moisture and is included in published disease-weather forecasting approaches.

leaf_wetness.notes: Leaf-wetness duration is an important component of FAST-type early-blight forecasting. Direct leaf-wetness may be unavailable from the weather API and may require proxy estimation.

wind.notes: Wind speed was included among meteorological predictors in the published Indian multi-location early-blight modelling study.

sunshine.notes: Bright sunshine duration was included as a predictor in the published Indian early-blight study.

published_model.model_type: Indian multi-location weather-based disease forecasting study with MLR and Support Vector Regression
published_model.output_interpretation: Prediction of early-blight disease severity using meteorological variables.
published_model.location_relevance: Strong Indian relevance, including a Maharashtra location (Rahuri), but raw training data and fitted deployment parameters are not available for direct reproduction.

rules.description: Temperature during prolonged wet or highly humid periods modifies early-blight infection risk.
Relative humidity >=90% increases moisture-related disease pressure.
Rainfall and prolonged leaf wetness increase infection suitability.
Recent or current confirmed disease presence increases case-specific risk.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: Disease severity forecasting evidence is strong, but a generalized farmer-facing yield-loss percentage has not yet been verified for the current pilot context.

limitations: The published Indian SVR model cannot be reproduced exactly without the original raw data and fitted parameters.
FAST-type models are external epidemiological models and require local calibration.
Weather-based risk should not be interpreted as guaranteed disease progression.

rules.description: Healthy image detection triggers preventive monitoring rather than disease treatment.
Environmental disease pressure may still be monitored for early blight, late blight and leaf mold.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: No crop-loss estimate is generated for a healthy detection.

limitations: A healthy leaf image does not prove that the entire tomato field is disease-free.
Environmental monitoring should continue when weather becomes favorable for major tomato diseases.

temperature.notes: Late-blight epidemiological models use temperature together with relative humidity, rainfall and wetness duration.

relative_humidity.notes: Periods of relative humidity above approximately 90% are commonly used in late-blight infection-period models.

rainfall.notes: Rainfall contributes to wetness and infection-period development. No universal rainfall cutoff is frozen.

leaf_wetness.notes: Prolonged moisture and wetness are key epidemiological drivers. Weather-API rainfall and humidity may be used only as proxies when measured leaf-wetness data are unavailable.

published_model.output_interpretation: Relative late-blight infection pressure under favorable weather conditions.
published_model.location_relevance: External epidemiological model; useful as a scientific rule framework but requires validation before calibrated use in Pune/Maharashtra.

rules.description: Sustained high relative humidity increases late-blight risk.
Temperature during humid/wet periods controls infection suitability.
Rainfall and prolonged wetness strengthen infection pressure.
Current late-blight detection substantially increases case-specific operational risk.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: Late blight can cause severe crop damage, but no generalized yield-loss percentage is frozen until crop-stage and regional impact literature are separately validated.

limitations: Current infection-period evidence is based on external models and requires local calibration.
Humidity and rainfall are imperfect proxies for actual canopy leaf wetness.
Risk output is environmental disease pressure, not a guaranteed infection probability.

temperature.notes: University extension guidance reports favorable leaf-mold development approximately in the 20–25°C range, with optimum around 22–24°C.

relative_humidity.notes: Relative humidity at or above approximately 85% strongly favors tomato leaf mold development.

rainfall.notes: Rainfall is not treated as a primary independent threshold. The major environmental driver is sustained high humidity, especially in protected or poorly ventilated cultivation.

leaf_wetness.notes: Persistent moisture and humid canopy conditions support disease development, although direct leaf-wetness duration is not frozen.

rules.description: Temperature approximately 20–25°C increases environmental suitability.
Relative humidity >=85% strongly increases leaf-mold risk.
Poor ventilation or protected cultivation can strengthen risk under persistent high humidity.
Current confirmed leaf-mold detection increases operational risk.

impact_evidence.evidence_notes: Current sources support environmental suitability and management guidance but do not provide a deployment-ready generalized yield-loss percentage.

limitations: Leaf mold risk is strongly influenced by protected cultivation, canopy density and ventilation.
External extension sources require local validation for Maharashtra conditions.
A prior supporting research paper involving Cladosporium cladosporioides is not treated as standalone evidence for Passalora fulva forecasting.
